chapters.title: Preface
paragraphs: I have gathered with care everything I could learn about the story of poor Werther, and I set it before you here, certain that you will thank me for it. You cannot withhold your admiration and love from his spirit and character, nor your tears from his fate.

And you, good soul, feeling the same anguish that once pressed on him — take comfort from his sorrows, and let this little book be your friend, if fate or your own fault leaves you no closer companion.

chapters.title: May 4, 1771
paragraphs: How glad I am to be away! Dear friend, what a strange thing the human heart is! To leave you — you whom I have been inseparable from, whom I love so dearly — and still to feel happy! I know you will forgive me. Weren't my other attachments practically appointed by fate to torment a mind like mine? Poor Leonora! And yet I was not to blame. Was it my fault that, while her sister's particular charms gave me such pleasant company, a passion took root in her own fragile heart? And yet — am I entirely innocent? Didn't I encourage her feelings? Didn't I delight in those wholly genuine expressions of nature that, though hardly comic in themselves, so often made us laugh? Didn't I — oh, what is a man, that he dares accuse himself like this? I promise you, dear friend, I will do better; I will no longer chew over every small misfortune that fate deals out, the way I always have; I will enjoy the present, and let the past stay past. You are right, of course, my best of friends — there would be far less suffering among us if people didn't work their imaginations so hard recalling old griefs, instead of bearing the present with some composure, though God knows why we are made this way. Please tell my mother I will handle her business as well as I can and send her word of it as soon as possible. I have seen my aunt, and she is nothing like the disagreeable woman our relatives make her out to be. She is lively and warm, with the kindest heart. I explained my mother's grievance about the part of her share that has been kept back. My aunt told me her own reasons and motives, and the terms on which she is willing to hand over the whole of it — and to do more than we asked. I can't write any more about it just now; only assure my mother that it will all come right. And once again, dear friend, this small affair has shown me that misunderstanding and neglect cause more trouble in the world than even malice and cruelty do. At least the last two are rarer.

Otherwise I am very well off here. Solitude in this earthly paradise is a soothing balm to my spirit, and this young spring warms my often anxious heart with all its generous promise. Every tree, every bush is a mass of blossom; you could wish yourself a butterfly, free to drift through this ocean of fragrance and find your whole life in it.

The town itself is unpleasant, but all around it lies an indescribable natural beauty. That is what moved the late Count M to lay out a garden on one of the sloping hills that cross each other here in the loveliest variety, forming the most charming valleys. The garden is simple, and the moment you enter you can tell it was not designed by a trained gardener but by a man who wanted a place to give himself up to his own feeling heart. I have already shed many a tear for its dead master in a summer-house that is now falling to ruin — his favorite spot, and now mine. Soon I will be master of the place myself. The gardener has taken to me these last few days, and he won't be the worse for it.

chapters.title: May 10, 1771
paragraphs: A wonderful calm has taken over my whole soul, like these sweet spring mornings that I enjoy with all my heart. I am alone, and glad to be alive in this place, which was made for souls like mine. I am so happy, dear friend, so lost in the sheer sense of quiet existence, that my art suffers for it. I couldn't draw a single line right now — and yet I have never been a greater painter than I am at this moment. When the lovely valley steams with mist around me, and the high midday sun rests on the surface of the dense canopy of my trees while only a few stray beams slip into the inner sanctuary, and I lie down in the tall grass beside the trickling stream — then, close to the earth, I notice a thousand small plants I had never seen; when I hear the hum of that little world among the stems and grow familiar with the countless strange shapes of the insects and the flies, then I feel the presence of the Almighty who made us in his own image, the breath of that all-embracing love that holds and carries us as it floats around us in an eternity of bliss. My friend! When the light then fails in my eyes, and the world around me and the sky above come to rest wholly in my soul like the face of a woman I love, I am often seized with longing, and think: oh, if only I could express this, could breathe onto paper all that lives so full and warm inside me, so that it might mirror my soul as my soul mirrors the infinite God! My friend — but it is beyond me; I go under, crushed by the sheer power of these visions.

chapters.title: May 12, 1771
paragraphs: I can't tell whether deceiving spirits hover over this place, or whether it is the warm, heavenly imagination in my own heart that turns everything around me into paradise. Just in front of the house there is a spring — a spring that holds me under a spell, like Melusina and her sisters. You go down a gentle slope and come to an archway, and some twenty steps further down the clearest crystal water gushes from the marble rock. The low wall that encloses it at the top, the tall trees that ring the spot, the coolness of the place itself — it all makes an impression at once pleasant and solemn. Not a day goes by that I don't spend an hour there. The young girls come out from town to fetch water — innocent, necessary work that once even kings' daughters did. When I sit and rest there, the old patriarchal life comes alive around me: I can see them, our forefathers, striking up friendships and arranging matches at the well, and I feel how kindly spirits watched over the springs and streams. Anyone who can't share these feelings has never really known the relief of resting by cool water after a hard summer's day.

chapters.title: May 13, 1771
paragraphs: You ask whether you should send me books. Dear friend, for the love of God, spare me that yoke! I don't want to be guided, stirred up, inflamed any more — my heart seethes quite enough on its own. What I need is something to lull me, and I find it perfectly in my Homer. How often I try to quiet the fever in my blood; you have never seen anything so changeable, so unsteady, as this heart of mine. But I hardly need confess that to you, who have so often had to watch me lurch from grief to wild joy, from sweet melancholy to violent passion. I treat my poor heart like a sick child and let it have whatever it wants. Don't repeat this — there are people who would hold it against me.

chapters.title: May 15, 1771
paragraphs: The common people here already know me and are fond of me — the children especially. When I first spent time with them and asked in a friendly way about their little affairs, some imagined I was mocking them and turned away in real ill humor. I didn't let it grieve me; I only felt, more sharply than ever, something I have often noticed before. People who can lay claim to a certain rank keep coldly aloof from the common folk, as if they feared losing their dignity by the contact; while frivolous idlers and the sort who like a cruel joke pretend to come down to their level, only to make the poor feel their insolence the more.

I know perfectly well that we are not all equal, and cannot be. But it is my view that a man who keeps his distance from the common people in order not to lose their respect is as much to blame as a coward who hides from his enemy for fear of losing.

The other day I went down to the spring and found a young servant girl who had set her pitcher on the bottom step and was looking round to see whether one of her friends was coming to help lift it onto her head. I went down and looked at her. "Shall I help you, my dear?" I said. She turned bright red. "Oh no, sir!" she said. "Don't stand on ceremony," I replied. She straightened the pad on her head, and I helped her. She thanked me and climbed the steps.

chapters.title: May 17, 1771
paragraphs: I have struck up all kinds of acquaintances, but found no real companionship yet. I don't know what it is about me that draws people; so many of them take to me and attach themselves to me, and it pains me when our paths only run together a little way. If you ask what the people here are like, I have to say: the same as everywhere. The human race is a monotonous business. Most of them spend the better part of their lives working just to stay alive, and the scrap of freedom that is left over frightens them so much that they will do anything to be rid of it. Oh, the lot of man!

But they are a thoroughly good sort. When I let myself go now and then and share the simple pleasures still left to ordinary people — sitting down, say, with real openness and good cheer at a well-laid table, or getting up a drive or a dance at the right moment, and so on — it does me a world of good; only I mustn't remember that so many other powers lie idle in me, rotting unused, that I have to keep carefully hidden. Ah, that thought wrings my heart. And yet to be misunderstood is the fate of people like us.

How sad that the friend of my youth is gone; how sad that I ever knew her! I could tell myself: you are a fool to look for what can't be found here on earth. But she was mine. I held that heart, that noble soul, and in her presence I seemed to be more than I was, because I was everything I could be. Good God — was a single power of my soul left unused? Couldn't I unfold, in front of her, the whole of that mysterious feeling with which my heart takes in nature? Wasn't our being together an endless weave of the finest feeling and the sharpest wit, whose every variation, even at its most playful, bore the mark of genius? And now — the few years she had over me carried her to the grave before me. I will never forget her steady mind, her heavenly patience.

A few days ago I met a young man named V—, a frank, open fellow with a very pleasant face. He has just come from the university; he doesn't think himself especially wise, but he does believe he knows more than other people. He has worked hard, as I can tell in all sorts of ways — in short, he is well informed. When he heard that I draw a good deal and that I know Greek (two rare things in this part of the country), he sought me out and unloaded his whole stock of learning, from Batteux to Wood, from De Piles to Winckelmann; he assured me he had read all the way through the first part of Sulzer's theory and owned a manuscript of Heyne's work on the study of antiquity. I let it all pass.

I have also got to know a very decent man, the district steward — a frank, warm-hearted soul. They tell me it is a real joy to see him among his children; he has nine, and his eldest daughter especially is much spoken of. He has invited me to visit, and I mean to go at the first chance. He lives at one of the prince's hunting lodges, an hour and a half's walk from here, which he was given leave to move into after his wife's death, since living in town and at the court was too painful for him.

A few other oddities of a dubious kind have also crossed my path — undesirable in every way, and most unbearable in their shows of friendship. Goodbye. You will like this letter: it is quite a chronicle.

chapters.title: May 22, 1771
paragraphs: That a man's life is only a dream — many have felt this before, and the feeling follows me everywhere too. When I see the narrow limits that pen in our active, searching powers; when I see how all our efforts go to providing for mere needs that themselves have no purpose beyond stretching out a poor existence; and how all our reassurance on certain questions we probe is just a dreamy resignation, while we paint the walls of our prison with bright figures and shining views — all this, Wilhelm, leaves me silent. I turn back into myself and find a world there — but more a world of intimation and dim longing than of clear, living force. And then everything blurs before my senses, and I go on through the world smiling and dreaming.

Every learned schoolmaster and tutor agrees that children don't know why they want what they want; but that grown men too should stagger about this earth like children, not knowing where they come from or where they are going, steered just as little by real purposes, led instead by biscuits and cakes and the birch — nobody likes to admit that, though it seems plain enough to me.

I know what you will say to this, and I am ready to grant that the happiest people are the ones who live for the day like children, who drag their dolls about and dress and undress them, who hang around the drawer where mother has locked up the sweets, and when they finally get their treat, gobble it down and cry "More!" Those are happy creatures. And there is another kind to be envied too — those who give their trifling occupations, even their passions, grand titles, and present them to the world as towering deeds done for its welfare and glory. Happy the man who can be like that! But anyone who humbly recognizes what all of this comes to; who sees how neatly the contented citizen trims his little garden into a paradise, how patiently even the poor man carries his load along his weary road, and how all of them want, equally, just to see the sunlight a little longer — he stays calm, and shapes his own world out of himself, and is happy too, because he is a human being. And then, hemmed in as he is, he still keeps in his heart that sweet feeling of freedom, and the knowledge that he can leave this prison whenever he chooses.

chapters.title: May 26, 1771
paragraphs: You know my old habit of settling in wherever I go — picking out a little cottage in some snug corner and putting up with every discomfort. Here too I have found just such a cosy, comfortable spot, one with its own peculiar charm for me.

About a league from the town there is a place called Walheim. (The reader needn't bother looking for the place under that name; we have had to change the real names given in the original.) It sits beautifully on the side of a hill, and if you follow one of the footpaths out of the village, you get a view of the whole valley. A good old woman lives there and keeps a little inn; she sells wine, beer, and coffee, and for all her age she is cheerful and pleasant. The real charm of the place is two linden trees that spread their huge branches over the small green in front of the church, which is ringed all around by peasants' cottages, barns, and farmyards. I have rarely seen anywhere so quiet and out of the way, and I often have my table and chair brought out from the inn and drink my coffee there and read my Homer. I happened on the spot one fine afternoon and found it completely deserted; everyone was out in the fields except a little boy of about four, who was sitting on the ground holding a baby of about six months between his knees, pressing it to his chest with both arms so that they made a kind of armchair. For all the liveliness sparkling in its dark eyes, the baby sat perfectly still. The sight charmed me. I sat down on a plough opposite and sketched this little picture of brotherly tenderness with real delight. I added the hedge nearby, the barn door, and a few broken cartwheels, just as they lay; and after about an hour I found I had made a well-composed, interesting drawing without putting in anything of my own. That confirmed me in my resolve to keep, from now on, entirely to nature. Nature alone is inexhaustible, and nature alone forms great masters. You can say a great deal in favor of rules — much the same as can be said for the conventions of society: a man trained on them will never produce anything downright bad or offensive, just as a man who keeps the law and minds his manners can never be an utterly unbearable neighbor or an outright villain. But say what you like, rules destroy the true feeling of nature and the true expression of it. You'll tell me that's too severe — that rules only restrain, only prune away rank growth, and so on. My good friend, let me give you an analogy. It is just like love. A warm-hearted young man gives himself wholly to a girl, spends every hour of the day with her, wears out his health and pours out his money to prove again and again that he is utterly devoted to her. Then along comes some man of the world, some man of office and standing, and says to him: "My dear young fellow, love is natural — but you must love within limits. Divide up your time: give part of it to your work and save your free hours for your sweetheart. Reckon up your money, and from whatever is left over you may make her a present — only not too often: on her birthday, say, and the like." If the young man takes this advice, he'll make a useful member of society, and I'd urge any prince to give him a post — but it's all over with his love, and, if he's an artist, with his art. Oh, my friend! Why is it that the torrent of genius so seldom breaks loose, so seldom comes roaring down in a full flood to shake your astonished soul? Because along both banks of the stream live cool, respectable people whose summer-houses and tulip beds would be ruined by it, and who therefore dig their channels and throw up their dikes in good time to head off the danger.

chapters.title: May 27, 1771
paragraphs: I see I have fallen into raptures and grand talk and similes, and so forgotten to tell you what became of the children. Wrapped up in my artistic musings, which I sketched out for you yesterday, I went on sitting on that plough for a good two hours. Toward evening a young woman came hurrying toward the children, who hadn't stirred the whole time, with a basket on her arm, calling out from a distance, "Philip, you've been such a good boy!" She greeted me; I returned it, got up, and went over. I asked whether she was the mother of these pretty children. "Yes," she said, and giving the older one a piece of bread, she picked up the baby and kissed it with all a mother's tenderness. "I left my little one in Philip's care," she said, "while I went into town with my eldest to buy some white bread and sugar and an earthenware pot." I could see all of it in the basket, the lid having slipped off. "I want to make some broth tonight for my little Hans" — the baby — "but that wild one, the eldest, smashed my pot yesterday squabbling with Philip over the scrapings." I asked after the eldest, and she had barely told me he was driving a couple of geese home from the meadow when he came running up and handed Philip a willow switch. I talked with the woman a while longer and learned that she was the schoolmaster's daughter, and that her husband had gone off to Switzerland to collect a legacy left him by a relative. "They tried to cheat him out of it," she said, "and wouldn't answer his letters, so he's gone there himself. I only hope nothing has happened to him; I've heard nothing since he left." I found it hard to leave the woman; I gave each of the children a kreutzer, and one more for the baby, so she could bring it some white bread for its broth next time she went to town, and we parted. I tell you, dear friend, when my thoughts are all in an uproar, the sight of a creature like this settles my troubled mind. She moves contentedly, without a care, around the small circle of her life, getting through one day at a time; and when she sees the leaves fall it means nothing to her but that winter is coming. Since then I've gone out there often. The children have grown quite used to me; they get sugar when I drink my coffee, and in the evening they share my bread and butter and milk. On Sundays they always get their kreutzer, for the good woman has orders to hand it to them when I'm not there after the evening service. They're entirely at ease with me and tell me everything, and I get special pleasure from watching their little tempers and the simplicity of their ways when a few of the other village children are gathered with them.
It cost me no end of trouble to set the mother's mind at rest, since she worried that they might "be a nuisance to the gentleman."

chapters.title: May 30, 1771
paragraphs: What I said the other day about painting holds just as true for poetry. The whole thing is simply to recognize what is truly excellent and dare to put it into words — and that says a great deal in a few. Today I had a scene that, told plainly, would make the loveliest idyll in the world. But why talk of poetry and scenes and idylls? Can we never just take pleasure in nature without dressing it up as art?

If after that opening you're expecting something grand or magnificent, you'll be badly let down. It's nothing more than a peasant lad who has stirred the warmest interest in me. As usual I'll tell it badly, and as usual you'll think I'm overdoing it. It's Walheim again — always Walheim — that produces these wonders.
A party had gathered outside the inn under the lindens to drink coffee. The company didn't quite suit me, so on one pretext or another I hung back.

A peasant came out of a nearby house and set about repairing part of the same plough I'd sketched a little while ago. I liked the look of him, so I spoke to him, asked about his situation, and we were soon acquainted — and, as usually happens with people of that class, he was soon confiding in me. He told me he was working for a young widow who thought very highly of him. He talked so much about his mistress and praised her so extravagantly that I could see at once he was head over heels in love with her. "She's no longer young," he said, "and her first husband treated her so badly that she has no intention of marrying again." From everything he said it was so plain what matchless charms she had for him, and how desperately he wished she would choose him to wipe out the memory of her first husband's cruelty, that I'd have to repeat his very words to give you any idea of the poor fellow's devotion, sincerity, and longing. I'd need a great poet's gifts to convey the play of his features, the music of his voice, the secret fire in his eyes. No words can capture the tenderness in his every movement and look; anything I might say would fall short. What touched me most was his anxiety that I might think badly of how things stood between him and his mistress, or doubt her good conduct. The charming way he described her figure and her person — which, though without the graces of youth, had drawn him to her and bound him fast — I can't reproduce; you'll have to imagine it. In all my life I've never seen, never pictured, never even thought possible, such intense devotion, such ardent longing, joined with so much purity. Don't blame me when I say that the memory of this innocence and truth has sunk deep into my soul, that this image of faithfulness and tenderness follows me everywhere, and that my own heart, as if kindled by the same flame, glows and burns within me.

I mean to go and see her as soon as I can — or rather, on second thought, perhaps I'd better not. Better to keep seeing her through her lover's eyes; to my own she might not look the way she stands before me now, and why spoil so sweet a picture?

chapters.title: June 16, 1771
paragraphs: "Why don't I write to you?" And you call yourself a learned man, asking that. You ought to have guessed that I'm well — in fact — in a word, I've met someone who has taken hold of my heart. I have — I hardly know.
To give you a proper, orderly account of how I came to know the most lovely of women would be beyond me. I'm happy and content, and a poor chronicler for it.
An angel! Nonsense — every man calls his sweetheart that. And yet I can't manage to tell you how perfect she is, or why she's so perfect; enough to say she has captured every one of my senses.
So much simplicity together with so much intelligence; so gentle, and yet so firm; a soul so serene, and a life so full of activity.

But all this is clumsy nonsense — abstractions that catch not a single trait of her, not one feature. Another time — no, not another time, now, this very instant, I'll tell you everything. Now or never. Well, just between us: since I started this letter I've three times been on the point of throwing down my pen, calling for my horse, and riding out — even though I swore this morning I wouldn't ride today, and even though I keep running to the window every other minute to see how high the sun has climbed.

I couldn't hold out — go to her I had to. Now I'm back, Wilhelm, and I'll write to you over my supper. What joy it was for my soul to see her surrounded by her dear, beautiful little brothers and sisters — eight of them!
But if I go on like this you'll be none the wiser at the end of the letter than at the start. So listen: I'll make myself give you the particulars.

I mentioned the other day that I'd got to know S—, the district steward, and that he'd invited me out to see him in his retreat — his little kingdom, rather. I put it off, and might never have gone if chance hadn't shown me the treasure hidden away in that quiet spot. Some of our young people had got up a country ball, and I agreed to go. I offered to escort a pretty, pleasant, but rather ordinary girl from the neighborhood, and it was settled that I'd hire a carriage and drive out with my partner and her aunt to collect Charlotte on the way. "You'll meet a very lovely young woman," my companion told me as we drove through the woods toward the hunting lodge. "Take care you don't lose your heart," the aunt added. "Why?" I asked. "Because she's already promised to a very fine man," she said, "who's away just now settling his affairs after his father's death, and stands to come into a sizable inheritance." The news meant nothing to me. As we reached the gate the sun was just going down behind the mountaintops. The air was heavy, and the ladies fretted about a storm coming on, with banks of low black cloud massing on the horizon. I soothed them by playing the weather prophet, though I had my own misgivings that our evening might be spoiled.

I got down, and a maid came to the door and asked us to wait a moment for her mistress. I crossed the courtyard to the handsome house, went up the front steps, and as I opened the door I saw the most charming sight I have ever laid eyes on. Six children, from eleven years old down to two, were rushing about the hall around a girl of middle height with a lovely figure, in a plain white dress trimmed with pink ribbons. She held a loaf of dark bread and was cutting slices for the little ones around her, each according to its age and appetite, handing them out with such grace and affection, every child waiting its turn with hands outstretched and shouting out its thanks. Some ran off at once with their supper, while the gentler ones walked out to the gate to look at the strangers and the carriage that was to carry their Charlotte away. "Do forgive me for making you come in for me, and for keeping the ladies waiting," she said. "What with dressing and arranging a few household things before I go out, I forgot to give the children their supper, and they won't take it from anyone but me." I made some empty compliment, but my whole soul was lost in her bearing, her voice, her way of moving, and I had barely collected myself when she darted into her room for her gloves and fan. The children eyed me from a little way off, and I went over to the youngest, the most delightful little creature. He drew back, and just then Charlotte came in and said, "Louis, give your cousin your hand." The little fellow did so readily, and I couldn't help giving him a hearty kiss in spite of his runny nose. "Cousin?" I said to Charlotte as I handed her down. "Do you think I deserve the good fortune of being related to you?" "Oh," she answered with an easy smile, "I have such a crowd of cousins that I'd be sorry to think you the least deserving of them." As she left she asked her next sister, Sophy, a girl of about eleven, to keep a close eye on the children and to say goodbye to their father for her when he got back from his ride. She told the little ones to mind their sister Sophy as if she were Charlotte herself, and some of them promised they would; but one fair-haired little girl of about six looked unhappy and said, "But Sophy isn't you, Charlotte, and we like you best." The two eldest boys had scrambled up onto the carriage, and at my request she let them ride a little way with us through the wood, on their promise to sit quite still and hold on tight.

We had barely settled in and the ladies barely finished their courtesies — the usual remarks on each other's dress and on the company we'd find — when Charlotte stopped the carriage and had her brothers climb down. They insisted on kissing her hand once more, the elder with all the tenderness of a boy of fifteen, the other more lightly and carelessly. She sent her love again to the children, and we drove on.

The aunt asked Charlotte whether she'd finished the book she'd sent her last. "No," said Charlotte, "I didn't care for it; you can have it back. And the one before wasn't much better." I was surprised, when I asked the title, to hear it was ——. (We feel bound to leave the title out of the letter, to spare anyone's feelings — though no author need set much store by the opinion of one young girl, or of an unsteady young man.)

Everything she said showed insight and character; with every remark her face seemed to light up with fresh charm, fresh sparks of spirit, that unfolded little by little as she felt herself understood.

"When I was younger," she said, "I loved nothing so much as novels. You can't imagine my delight when I could settle into a corner on some quiet holiday and throw myself heart and soul into the joys and sorrows of some made-up Leonora. I won't pretend that kind of book has lost all its charm for me even now. But since I read so seldom, I want books exactly to my taste. And I like best the authors whose world is my own — books about the life around me, about the people I know, whose stories grip me because they're so like my own plain existence, which, without being paradise, is on the whole a source of happiness I can't put into words."

I tried to hide how those words moved me, with little success; for when she went on to speak so truly about The Vicar of Wakefield and other books — whose names I'll leave out (the authors named deserve Charlotte's praise and will feel it in their hearts when they read this; no one else need mind) — I couldn't hold myself in any longer and said exactly what I thought. It was only when Charlotte turned to the other two ladies that I noticed they'd been sitting there wide-eyed the whole time, hearing nothing of it. The aunt gave me more than one mocking glance, which I didn't mind in the least.

We talked of the pleasures of dancing. "If it's a fault to love it," said Charlotte, "then I freely own I prize dancing above every other amusement. Whenever something is troubling me, I go and drum out a dance I've danced on my out-of-tune piano, and at once everything is right again."

You, who know me, can imagine how I fixed my eyes on those rich dark ones of hers as she said all this, how my whole soul hung on her warm lips and fresh, glowing cheeks, how, lost in the lovely sense of what she meant, I often hardly caught the words themselves. In short — you know me — I stepped down from the carriage like a man in a dream, so lost to the dusk-lit world around me that I barely heard the music drifting down from the lit-up ballroom.

Two gentlemen named Audran and a certain N.N. — I can't be bothered with all the names — who were the aunt's and Charlotte's partners, met us at the carriage door and carried off their ladies, while I led mine upstairs.

We began with minuets. I led out one lady after another, and of course it was exactly the most tiresome ones who couldn't bring themselves to give me back my hand and have done. Charlotte and her partner started an English country dance, and you can imagine my delight when it came to her turn to do the figure with us. You ought to see Charlotte dance! She dances with her whole heart and soul; her whole body is one harmony, so carefree and easy, as if dancing were everything, as if she thought and felt nothing else — and surely in that moment everything else does fall away.

She was engaged for the second country dance but promised me the third, and assured me with the most charming frankness that she loved to waltz. "It's the custom here," she said, "for partners to waltz together, but mine waltzes badly and will thank me for sparing him the trouble. Your lady can't waltz and doesn't care to either, but I saw during the country dance that you waltz well; so if you'd like to waltz with me, go and ask my partner's leave, and I'll go and ask your lady's." We agreed, and arranged that her partner should keep my lady company in the meantime.

Off we went, and at first delighted in the graceful play of the arms. With what grace, what lightness she moved! When the waltz proper began and the couples went wheeling round one another, there was some confusion at first, since several of the dancers weren't up to it. We sensibly held back and let them tire themselves out, and once the clumsy ones had dropped away we joined in and kept it up splendidly, along with one other couple, Audran and his partner. I have never danced so lightly in my life. I was no longer a mere man. To hold the loveliest of creatures in my arms and fly with her like the wind, until everything else around us vanished — Wilhelm, to be honest, I swore to myself in that moment that a girl I loved, that I had any claim on, should never waltz with anyone but me, though it cost me my soul. You'll understand.

We took a few turns about the room to get our breath. Then Charlotte sat down, and the oranges I'd managed to put aside — the last ones left — did her good; only, every slice she politely offered to a greedy neighbor beside her went through my heart like a knife.

In the third country dance we were the second couple. As we were going down the line — and heaven knows with what rapture I hung on her arm and her eyes, brimming with the purest, frankest delight — we passed a woman whose lovely, kindly face had caught my eye, though she was no longer young. She looked at Charlotte with a smile, raised a warning finger, and as we flew past said the name "Albert" twice, with great meaning.

"Who is Albert," I asked Charlotte, "if it's not rude to ask?" She was just about to answer when we had to part to make a figure, and as we crossed in front of each other again I thought she looked a little pensive. "Why should I hide it from you?" she said, giving me her hand for the promenade. "Albert is a fine man, and I'm as good as engaged to him." Now this was no news to me — the girls had told me on the way out — and yet it struck me as wholly new, because I hadn't yet thought of it in connection with her, who in so short a time had come to mean so much to me. At any rate I lost my head, lost my place in the figure, and threw the whole set into confusion, so that it took all Charlotte's composure, pulling and pushing me, to get me right again.

The dance wasn't over when the lightning that had been flickering on the horizon for a while — which I'd insisted was only heat lightning — grew fierce, and the thunder drowned the music. When fear or alarm catches us in the middle of our pleasures it always strikes deeper than usual, whether because the contrast makes us feel it more keenly, or, more likely, because our senses are wide open just then and the shock goes in harder. To this I lay the panic and shrieks of the ladies. One cleverly sat down in a corner with her back to the window and her fingers in her ears; another knelt before her and hid her face in the first one's lap; a third pushed in between them and threw her arms around her sister, weeping buckets. Some wanted to go home; others, scarcely knowing what they did, had too little presence of mind to fend off the cheek of their young partners, who were busy intercepting for themselves the frightened prayers our trembling beauties meant for heaven. Some of the men had slipped downstairs for a quiet pipe, and the rest of us gladly took up the hostess's happy suggestion of moving into another room with shutters and curtains. We'd hardly got there when Charlotte set the chairs in a ring and, once everyone had sat down at her bidding, proposed a game.

I saw more than one person pucker up and stretch in pleasant anticipation of a forfeit. "Let's play counting," said Charlotte. "Now pay attention. I'll go round the circle from right to left, and each of you in turn calls out his number — count quickly; whoever hesitates or slips gets a box on the ear, and so on up to a thousand." It was a joy to watch. She went round the ring with her arm raised. "One," said the first; "two," the next; "three," the third; and so on, while she went faster and faster. Then someone slipped — smack, a box on the ear — and amid the laughter the next one slipped too, and so on, faster and faster. I caught two boxes myself, and was delighted to fancy they were harder than the rest. A general burst of laughter and uproar broke the game off well before we reached a thousand. The party drifted apart into little knots; the storm had passed, and I followed Charlotte back into the ballroom. On the way she said, "The forfeits made them forget all about the storm." I couldn't say a word. "I was as frightened as any of them," she went on, "but by acting brave to keep the others' courage up I forgot my own fear." We went to the window. Thunder was still rolling in the distance; a soft rain was falling over the land, and the most delicious fragrance rose to us on the warm air. She stood there leaning on her elbow, her gaze searching the countryside; she looked up at the sky and then at me, her eyes full of tears; she laid her hand on mine and said, "Klopstock!" At once I knew the magnificent ode in her mind, and I sank under the flood of feeling that the one word loosed in me. It was more than I could bear. I bent over her hand and kissed it through tears of bliss, and looked again into her eyes. Noble poet! If only you could have seen your worship in that look — and may I never again hear your name, so often profaned, on lesser lips!

chapters.title: June 19, 1771
paragraphs: I no longer know where I broke off the story; all I know is that it was two in the morning when I got to bed, and that if I could have talked to you instead of writing, I'd very likely have kept you up till dawn.

I don't think I've told you yet what happened on the drive home from the ball — and I haven't time now either. It was the most glorious sunrise: the dripping wood, the freshened country all around. Our companions had dozed off. Charlotte asked whether I didn't want to sleep too, and begged me not to stay awake on her account. "As long as I can see those eyes open," I said, looking straight at her, "there's no danger of my falling asleep." We both stayed awake right to her door. The maid let us in softly and assured her, in answer to her questions, that her father and the children were well and still asleep. I left her, asking leave to call on her later that same day. She gave it, and I went; and since then sun, moon, and stars may go about their business as they please — I don't know whether it's day or night, and the whole world has melted away around me.

chapters.title: June 21, 1771
paragraphs: My days are as happy as the ones God keeps for his saints; and whatever becomes of me, no one can ever say I haven't known joy — the purest joy of life. You know Walheim. I'm fully settled there now. From there it's only half a league to Charlotte; there I feel myself, and taste all the happiness a man can be given.

Little did I think, when I picked Walheim as the goal of my walks, that heaven itself lay so close by. How often, on my long rambles — from the hilltop, from the meadow across the river — have I looked out at that hunting lodge, which now holds everything my heart could wish.

I've often thought, dear Wilhelm, about the longing that drives men to roam and seek out new things, and then about the quiet pull that draws them back afterward to their narrow round, to fall in with custom and trouble themselves no more about the wider world.

It's so strange: when I first came here and looked out over the lovely valley from the hill, how it all drew me — the little wood there, how good to sit in its shade; that peak, what a view from it; that chain of gentle hills and the snug valleys at their feet — oh, to lose myself wandering among them! And I went, and came back, and hadn't found what I'd hoped. Distance, my friend, is like the future. A great dim whole lies spread before our soul; our feeling blurs into it as our sight does, and we long to give our whole self up and be filled to the brim with the bliss of one single, vast, glorious feeling. But alas — when we hurry toward it, when there becomes here, everything is just as it was, and we stand as poor and hemmed-in as ever, our soul thirsting still for the happiness that slipped away.

So even the most restless wanderer comes in the end to long for home, and finds in his own cottage, on his wife's breast, among his children, and in the work of providing for them, the happiness he chased in vain across the wide world.

When I walk out to Walheim at sunrise and there in the garden pick my own peas for dinner, and sit down to shell them while I read my Homer between handfuls; when I choose a pot in the little kitchen, cut myself a pat of butter, set my peas on the fire, cover them, and sit by to give them a stir now and then — I can feel so vividly how Penelope's overbearing suitors slaughtered and carved and roasted their own oxen and swine. Nothing fills me with so quiet and true a sense of happiness as these touches of patriarchal life, which, thank heaven, I can weave into my own without affectation. How glad I am that my heart can feel the simple, harmless joy of a man who brings to his table a cabbage he grew himself, and who in that one moment relives not just the cabbage but all the good days — the fine morning he planted it, the soft evenings he watered it, the pleasure he took in watching it grow — all of it together again.

chapters.title: June 29, 1771
paragraphs: The day before yesterday the doctor came out from town to see the steward and found me on the floor among Charlotte's children, some of them climbing over me, others teasing me, while I tickled them and we all made a great racket. The doctor is a very stiff sort of man; he keeps adjusting the pleats of his cuffs and tweaking his frill while he talks to you, and he plainly thought such carrying-on beneath the dignity of a sensible man — I could read it in his face. But I didn't let it put me off; I let him go on with his weighty talk while I rebuilt the children's card houses for them as fast as they knocked them down. And sure enough he went round town afterward complaining that the steward's children were spoiled enough already, but that now Werther was ruining them altogether.

Yes, dear Wilhelm, nothing on this earth touches my heart like children. When I watch them, and see in the little creatures the seeds of every virtue, every strength they'll one day so badly need; when I make out in the stubborn child the firmness and steadiness of a fine character to come, and in the unruly one the good humor and lightness that will carry him safely over life's dangers — and all of it still whole, still unspoiled — then I say over to myself again and again the golden words of the Teacher of mankind: "Unless you become as one of these!" And yet, my friend, these children, who are our equals, whom we ought to take as our models, we treat as our subjects. They're to have no will of their own. And have we none, then? Where does our great privilege come from? Because we're older and wiser? Good God in heaven, you see only big children and little children, and nothing else; and your Son said long ago which give you the greater joy. But they believe in him and don't listen to him — that too is an old story — and they shape their children after themselves, and so on.
Goodbye, Wilhelm; I won't muddle my head any further with this.

chapters.title: July 1, 1771
paragraphs: The comfort Charlotte can bring to a sick friend, I feel in my own heart, which suffers more from being apart from her than many a poor soul wasting away in bed. She's spending a few days in town with a worthy woman whom the doctors have given up, and who wants Charlotte near her at the end. Last week I went with her to visit the vicar of St—, a little village up in the hills about a league from here. We got there around four; Charlotte had brought her little sister along. As we came into the vicarage yard we found the good old man sitting on a bench by the door under the shade of two big walnut trees. At the sight of Charlotte he seemed to come to life, forgot his stick, and made to get up and walk toward her. She ran to him and made him sit down again, took a seat beside him, passed on a great many messages from her father, and then scooped up his youngest, an ugly, grubby little thing, the darling of his old age, and kissed it. I wish you could have seen how she gave herself to that old man — raising her voice for his deafness, telling him of strong young people carried off without warning, praising the waters at Carlsbad, approving his plan to spend the coming summer there, telling him he looked better and stronger than the last time she saw him. I, meanwhile, paid my respects to his wife. The old man grew quite cheerful, and since I couldn't help admiring the fine walnut trees that shaded us so pleasantly, he began, with a little effort, to tell us their story. "The older one," he said, "we don't know who planted — some say this parson, some that. But the younger one behind us is exactly my wife's age: fifty next October. Her father planted it the morning of the day she was born that evening. He was my predecessor here, and there's no telling how he loved that tree — and it's just as dear to me. My wife was sitting under it on a beam, knitting, when I first walked into this yard, a poor student, twenty-seven years ago." Charlotte asked after his daughter, and he said she'd gone out to the meadows with Herr Schmidt to see the haymakers, and then went on with his story: how his predecessor had taken a liking to him, and the daughter too, and how he'd become first the man's curate and then his successor. He'd barely finished when the daughter came back through the garden with this Herr Schmidt. She gave Charlotte a warm welcome, and I'll admit I rather liked her — a lively, good-natured brunette, the sort who could keep you amused for a while in the country. Her suitor (for that's plainly what Schmidt was) was a polite but reserved fellow who wouldn't join our talk however hard Charlotte tried to draw him out. What annoyed me most was seeing in his face that it was temper, not dullness, that kept him silent. This came out clearly later: when we set off on a walk and Frederica fell in beside Charlotte, and so beside me, the man's face, naturally rather dark, grew so black and sullen that Charlotte had to pluck my sleeve and warn me I was paying Frederica too much attention. Now nothing in the world vexes me more than to see people torment one another — above all when the young, in the very flower of life, in the very season for joy, throw away their few bright days on quarrels, and only see what they've done when it's too late to mend it. It weighed on me, and that evening, back at the vicarage and sitting round the table over our bread and milk, when the talk turned to the joys and sorrows of the world, I couldn't help laying into ill-humor. "We're forever complaining," I said, "that good days are so few and bad days so many — and usually with little reason. If our hearts were always open to take in the good that heaven sends us, we'd have the strength to bear the bad when it comes." "But we can't command our moods," said the vicar's wife. "So much depends on the body; when you're out of sorts physically, nothing feels right." "Granted," I said, "but then let's treat it as an illness and ask whether there isn't a cure."

"That makes sense," said Charlotte. "At least I think a great deal depends on us; I know it does with me. When something nettles me and threatens to sour my mood, I jump up and pace the garden singing a couple of dance tunes, and it's gone at once." "That's just what I meant," I said. "Ill-humor is exactly like idleness — it comes naturally to us — but once we find the courage to rouse ourselves, the work flies along and we discover a real pleasure in the activity we'd been shrinking from." Frederica was listening closely, and the young man objected that we aren't masters of ourselves, still less of our feelings. "We're talking about a disagreeable feeling," I answered, "that everyone would be glad to escape — and no one knows how far his own strength reaches until he tries. Surely a sick man will gladly consult every doctor, and not refuse the strictest diet or the bitterest medicine, to get his health back." I noticed the good old vicar leaning in, straining to follow, so I raised my voice and turned to him directly. "We preach against all sorts of vices," I said, "but I've never yet heard a sermon against ill-humor." "The town clergy might manage that," he said; "country folk are never out of temper — though now and then it mightn't hurt, as a tonic for my wife, say, and the steward." We all laughed, and he laughed heartily too, until a coughing fit took him and broke off our talk for a while. Then Herr Schmidt picked it up again. "You call ill-humor a vice," he said, "but I think that's putting it too strongly." "Not at all," I replied, "if it deserves the name for the harm it does us and those around us. Isn't it enough that we can't make one another happy — must we also rob each other of the little happiness each heart might find on its own? Show me the man so out of temper who has the strength to hide it, to carry it alone without poisoning the peace of everyone near him! No — ill-humor springs from an inward sense of our own unworthiness, from a discontent forever tangled up with the envy that foolish vanity breeds. We see people happy whom we didn't make so, and we can't stand it." Charlotte smiled at me, seeing the feeling I spoke with, and a tear in Frederica's eye spurred me on. "Woe to those," I said, "who use their power over another heart to rob it of the simple joys it would have had on its own! All the gifts and attentions in the world can't buy back one moment's pleasure that a jealous tyranny has spoiled at its source." My heart was full as I spoke; the memory of much that had happened pressed on me and brought tears to my eyes. "We should tell ourselves every day," I cried, "that we owe our friends nothing but to leave them their own joys and to deepen their happiness by sharing it. When their souls are racked by some violent passion, or torn with grief, can you give them one drop of comfort?

"And when the last fatal illness fastens on the woman whose early grave you helped dig, and she lies there spent and failing, her dim eyes turned to heaven and the sweat of death on her pale forehead — you stand at the foot of the bed like a condemned man, knowing in your bones that all you have could do nothing to save her, wrung by the thought that nothing in your power can pour even a flicker of strength into the sinking soul, one last spark of comfort."

At those words the memory of just such a scene I'd once stood through broke over me with full force. I pressed my handkerchief to my eyes and hurried out of the room, and only came back to myself at Charlotte's voice calling that it was time to go home. And how she scolded me on the way, so tenderly, for taking everything too much to heart — that it would be the ruin of me, that I must spare myself! Oh my angel — for your sake I will.

chapters.title: July 6, 1771
paragraphs: She's still with her dying friend, and still the same bright, lovely creature who eases pain and scatters happiness wherever she turns. Yesterday evening she went walking with her little sisters; I knew it, met them, and we went on together. After about an hour and a half we turned back toward town. We stopped at the spring I love so much — now a thousand times dearer to me than before. Charlotte sat down on the low wall and we gathered round her. I looked about me, and the time when my heart was still free and empty came back to me. "Dear spring," I said, "since then I've never once come to rest by your cool water; sometimes, hurrying past, I haven't even glanced at you." I looked down and saw Charlotte's little sister Jane coming up the steps with a glass of water. I turned to Charlotte, and felt all over again what she is to me. Just then Jane came up with the glass, and her sister Marianne tried to take it from her. "No!" the child cried, with the sweetest look, "no — Charlotte must drink first!"

The affection, the simplicity in the way she said it carried me away so that I couldn't find any way to show what I felt but to snatch the child up and kiss her warmly — at which she screamed and burst into tears. "You shouldn't have done that," said Charlotte. I stood there at a loss. "Come, Jane," she went on, taking her by the hand and leading her down the steps, "never mind — quick, wash it off in the fresh water, quick." I stood watching as the little thing scrubbed away at her cheeks with her wet hands, certain that the miraculous water would rinse off every trace of contamination from my ugly stubble; and though Charlotte said that was enough, she kept scrubbing with all her might, as if too much were safer than too little. I tell you, Wilhelm, I never stood at a baptism with more reverence; and when Charlotte came back up I could have bowed down before her as before a prophet who had washed away a nation's sins.

That evening, in the joy of my heart, I couldn't keep from telling the story to a man I credited with some natural feeling, since he has a good head on him. But how wrong I was! He held that Charlotte had done quite wrong — that we mustn't fool children, that such things lead to no end of errors and superstitions we're bound to guard the young against. It struck me just then that the man had had a child christened only the week before, so I let it drop, and in my heart held to the truth: we ought to deal with children as God deals with us, who makes us happiest of all when he lets us reel along inside a pleasant illusion.

chapters.title: July 8, 1771
paragraphs: What a child a man is, to set such store by a glance! What a child a man is! We'd gone out to Walheim. The ladies drove, and during our walk I thought I saw, in Charlotte's dark eyes — I'm a fool, forgive me, but you should see them, those eyes! To keep it short, since my own eyes are heavy with sleep: well, the ladies were getting back into the carriage, and young W., Selstadt, Audran, and I stood about the door. They're a lively lot, all laughing and bantering. I watched Charlotte's eyes; they went from one to another — but not to me, to me, who stood there fixed on her and nothing else! My heart said goodbye to her a thousand times, and she never looked at me. The carriage rolled off, and tears stood in my eyes. I gazed after it — and then I saw Charlotte's bonnet lean out of the window, and she turned to look back. At me? Ah, dear friend, I can't be sure, and in that not knowing lies my comfort. Perhaps she turned for me. Perhaps! Goodnight. Oh, what a child I am!

chapters.title: July 10, 1771
paragraphs: You should see what a fool I cut in company when her name comes up — especially when someone asks me point-blank how I like her. Like her! I loathe the word. What kind of man could merely like Charlotte, and not have his whole heart and senses swallowed up by her? Like her! Someone asked me the other day how I "like" Ossian!

chapters.title: July 11, 1771
paragraphs: Madame M— is very ill. I pray she'll recover, because Charlotte suffers along with her. I see Charlotte now and then at my friend's house, and today she told me the strangest thing. Old M— is a grasping, tight-fisted fellow who has long pinched and plagued the poor woman, though she's borne it patiently. A few days ago, when the doctor told us there was no hope for her, she sent for her husband — Charlotte was in the room — and said to him: "I have something to confess that could cause trouble and confusion after I'm gone. I've kept your house as thriftily and carefully as I could all these years — but you'll have to forgive me for cheating you for thirty of them. When we were first married you set aside a small sum for the kitchen and the other household needs. As our household grew and our means with it, I could never get you to raise the weekly housekeeping to match; you know that even when our needs were greatest you insisted I run everything on seven florins a week. I took the money without a word and made up the difference each week out of the cash box, since no one would suspect the mistress of robbing the till. I've wasted nothing, and I could have gone to meet my Maker without saying any of this — except that whoever takes over the house after me won't know how to manage, and you'll keep insisting that your first wife got by on the same sum."

I talked it over with Charlotte — how unbelievably men can blind themselves, that anyone could fail to suspect something was wrong when seven florins were meant to cover costs twice that. But I've known people myself who'd have taken the prophet's never-emptying jar of oil into their own house without batting an eye.

chapters.title: July 13, 1771
paragraphs: No, I'm not deceiving myself. In her dark eyes I read a genuine feeling for me and for what becomes of me. Yes — I feel it, and in this I dare trust my own heart — that she — oh, dare I speak it, dare I say the words that hold heaven in them? — that she loves me!
That she loves me! And how precious I have become to myself, how — to you I can say it, you'll understand such things — how I worship myself, since she loves me!

Is this presumption, or a true sense of how things stand? I don't know the man I'd fear as a rival in Charlotte's heart; and yet, when she speaks of her betrothed with such warmth, such affection, I feel like a soldier stripped of his rank and honors and stripped of his sword.

chapters.title: July 16, 1771
paragraphs: How my heart pounds when by chance my finger brushes hers, or our feet meet under the table! I pull back as if from a furnace, and a secret pull draws me forward again, and my head swims. Oh, her innocent, open heart has no idea what torment these little intimacies put me through. And when, in the thick of talk, she lays her hand on mine and leans closer to me, so that the heavenly breath of her mouth reaches my lips — I feel as if struck by lightning, ready to drop where I stand. And yet, Wilhelm, if I ever dared — with all this heaven, all this trust — if I ever dared to — you understand me. No, no — my heart isn't so far gone. Weak — yes, weak enough. And isn't that already a kind of corruption?

She is sacred to me. Every desire falls silent in her presence. I never know what I feel when I'm near her; it's as if my soul turned over in every nerve of my body. There's a melody she plays on the piano with the touch of an angel — so simple and so full of spirit! It's her favorite tune, and the moment she strikes the first note all my pain, confusion, and brooding lift away.

Not a word that's ever been said about the old magic of music seems unlikely to me now. How that simple song takes hold of me! And how well she knows when to play it — often just when I feel like putting a bullet through my head. The darkness and madness in me scatter, and I breathe more freely again.

chapters.title: July 18, 1771
paragraphs: Wilhelm, what is the world to our hearts without love? A magic lantern without its lamp. The moment you set the little flame inside it, the brightest pictures shine out on your white wall! And even if they're nothing but passing phantoms, still it makes us happy when we stand before them like children, carried away by the wonderful sight. Today I couldn't get to Charlotte — visitors I couldn't shake off held me back. What was I to do? I sent my servant over, just to have someone near me today who'd been near her. How impatiently I waited for him, how overjoyed I was to see him back! I'd have caught him up and kissed him, if I hadn't been ashamed.

They say the Bologna stone, set out in the sun, drinks in its rays and glows for a while afterward in the dark. It was just so with me and the boy. The thought that her eyes had rested on his face, his cheeks, the buttons of his coat and the collar of his jacket, made all of it so sacred, so precious, that in that moment I wouldn't have given him up for a thousand thalers. I felt so happy in his presence. God forbid you laugh at me, Wilhelm. Can it be a delusion, if it makes us happy?

chapters.title: July 19, 1771
paragraphs: "I'm going to see her!" I cry first thing in the morning, looking up cheerfully at the glorious sun. "I'm going to see her!" And then I've no other wish for the whole day. Everything, everything is swallowed up in that one prospect.

chapters.title: July 20, 1771
paragraphs: I can't agree to your idea that I should go with the ambassador to ——. I have no love for taking orders, and besides, we all know the man is an unpleasant brute to deal with. My mother would like to see me employed, you say — that made me laugh. Am I not employed now? And what's the real difference whether I'm counting peas or lentils? Everything in the world comes down in the end to a trifle, and a man who wears himself out for the sake of others, chasing money or honors or whatever else, without a passion or a need of his own to drive him, is a fool.

chapters.title: July 24, 1771
paragraphs: You press me so hard not to neglect my drawing that I'd rather say nothing at all than admit how little I've done lately.

Never have I been happier, never have I felt nature more fully, down to the smallest pebble, the smallest blade of grass — and yet I can't find any way to put it out. My powers of execution have deserted me; everything floats and shimmers before my soul so that I can't seize a single clean outline. But I keep fancying I'd do better with clay or wax to work in. If this lasts much longer I'll get some clay and knead away, even if all that comes of it is dumplings.

I've begun Charlotte's portrait three times now, and three times made a fool of myself — which galls me all the more because not long ago I had a real gift for taking likenesses. So in the end I just cut out her silhouette, and I'll have to make do with that.

chapters.title: July 25, 1771
paragraphs: Yes, dear Charlotte, I'll see to everything and arrange it all; only give me more errands, the more the better. One thing, though, I must ask: no more blotting-sand on the little notes you write me. Today I raised your letter quickly to my lips, and it set my teeth grinding.

chapters.title: July 26, 1771
paragraphs: Many a time I've resolved not to see her so often. But who could keep such a vow! Every day I give in to the temptation, swearing faithfully that tomorrow, for once, I'll stay away — and when tomorrow comes I find some irresistible reason all over again, and before I know how, I'm with her. Either she's said the evening before, "You'll come tomorrow, won't you?" — and who could stay away after that? — or she gives me an errand, and I find it only proper to bring her the answer myself; or the day is too fine, and I walk out to Walheim, and once I'm there it's only half a league more to her — and I'm too close to the spell not to be drawn in, and there I am with her again. My grandmother used to tell us a tale of a magnetic mountain: any ship that sailed too near it was stripped of all its iron in an instant, the nails flying off to the mountain, and the poor sailors went down among the collapsing planks.

chapters.title: July 30, 1771
paragraphs: Albert has arrived, and now I must go. Were he the best, the noblest of men, a man I'd gladly put above myself in every way, I still couldn't bear to watch him possess such perfection before my eyes. Possess — enough, Wilhelm: the betrothed is here. A fine, good-hearted fellow you can't help but like. Luckily I wasn't there when they met — it would have torn my heart apart. And he's so considerate; he hasn't kissed Charlotte once in my presence. Heaven reward him for it! I have to love him for the respect he shows her. He's kindly disposed toward me, though I suspect that's Charlotte's doing more than his own feeling. Women have a fine touch in these things, and rightly so — it's all to their good if they can keep two admirers on good terms, however seldom they manage it.

All the same, I can't help respecting Albert. His outward calm stands in sharp relief against my own restlessness, which I can't hide. He has plenty of feeling and knows full well what a treasure he has in Charlotte. He seems free of ill-humor, and you know that's the failing I hate above all others in a man.

He takes me for a man of sense; and my devotion to Charlotte, the warm delight I take in everything she does, only swells his triumph, and he loves her the more for it. Whether he doesn't now and then needle her with a little jealousy I'll leave aside; in his place I certainly wouldn't be entirely safe from that devil myself.

Be that as it may — my joy in being near Charlotte is gone. Shall I call it folly, or blindness? What's in a name? The thing speaks for itself! I knew everything I know now before Albert came; I knew I had no claim to make on her, and I made none — that is, so far as it's possible not to ache with longing in the presence of so much loveliness. And now the fool stands here goggling, because another man has actually turned up and is carrying the girl off.

I grind my teeth and mock my own misery — and I'd mock twice over anyone who told me to resign myself, since nothing can be done. Spare me these straw men! I run through the woods, and when I come to Charlotte and find Albert sitting beside her in the little garden arbor, and I can't go on, I turn wild and play the fool and get up to a hundred follies. "For God's sake," Charlotte said to me today, "no more scenes like last night, I beg you! You frighten me when you're so worked up." Between us — I watch now for the hours he's away on business, and off I go, and I'm always happy when I find her alone.

chapters.title: August 8, 1771
paragraphs: Believe me, dear Wilhelm, I didn't mean you when I spoke so harshly of the people who tell us to bow to the inevitable. I truly never thought you might hold such a view. And at bottom you're right. Only one thing, my friend: in this world it's very seldom a matter of either-or. Feelings and ways of acting have as many gradations as there are shades of nose between a hooked one and a snub.
So you'll allow me to grant your whole argument and still try to slip out between its horns.

It comes to this, you say: either you have some hope of winning Charlotte, or you have none. Good — in the first case, push on and try to bring your wish to fruit; in the second, pull yourself together and try to be rid of a wretched feeling that will eat up all your strength. My dear fellow — well said, and easily said.

But would you ask a poor wretch whose life is being slowly gnawed away by a creeping illness to put a quick end to his torment with one stroke of the knife? Doesn't the very disease that drains his strength also rob him of the courage to free himself?
You could answer me with a kindred analogy: who wouldn't rather have his arm taken off than risk his life by hesitating and hanging back? I don't know. But let's not trade comparisons any longer.
Enough. There are moments, Wilhelm, when I could leap up and shake the whole thing off, and then, if only I knew where to, I think I would go.
That same evening.

My diary, which I've let lie for a while, came into my hands again today, and I'm amazed how knowingly I walked into all of this, step by step. To have seen my situation so clearly the whole time, and yet to have behaved like a child — to see it even now, plainly, and still show no sign of growing any wiser.

chapters.title: August 10, 1771
paragraphs: I could be living the happiest, finest life here, if only I weren't a fool. Such pleasant circumstances, and so well suited to delight a man's soul, rarely come together. Ah — how true it is that the heart alone makes our happiness. To be part of this lovely family; loved by the old man like a son, by the little ones like a father, and by Charlotte — and then the good Albert, who never spoils my happiness with any sour mood, but takes me in with the warmest friendship, and after Charlotte loves me best in the world! Wilhelm, it's a joy to hear the two of us on our walks, talking about Charlotte. Nothing more absurd than this whole arrangement was ever invented in the world, and yet it often brings tears to my eyes.

He tells me about her good mother — how on her deathbed she handed over her house and children to Charlotte, and Charlotte herself to him; how from that day a new spirit had filled the girl, how in her care and worry over the household she became a true mother to them, how not one moment of her time passed without active love and work, and yet her cheerfulness and her light heart never left her. I walk along beside him, picking flowers by the path, weaving them carefully into a little wreath, and then — throwing it into the stream as it runs by, watching it bob gently away downstream. I don't know whether I told you that Albert is to stay here; he's been given a post at court with a good salary, and stands high in favor there. In matters of business I've met few people so orderly and exact.

chapters.title: August 12, 1771
paragraphs: Albert is certainly the best fellow alive. I had a strange scene with him yesterday. I'd gone to take my leave, since the whim took me to ride up into these hills, from which I'm writing to you now. As I was pacing his room my eye fell on his pistols. "Lend me the pistols," I said, "for the journey." "Gladly," he said, "if you'll take the trouble to load them; they only hang there for show." I took one down, and he went on, "Ever since my caution played me such a nasty trick, I won't have anything more to do with the things." I was curious to hear the story. "I was staying about three months," he said, "at a friend's place in the country. I had a pair of unloaded pocket-pistols, and slept easy. One rainy afternoon, sitting about with nothing to do, it came into my head — I don't know how — that we might be attacked, that we might need the pistols, that — well, you know how it goes when one has nothing better to do. I handed them to the servant to clean and load. He was fooling with the maid, trying to scare her, and somehow — God knows how — the gun went off, the ramrod still down the barrel, and drove it into the ball of her right thumb and smashed it. So I had her wailing to put up with and the surgeon's bill to pay into the bargain, and ever since I've kept my weapons unloaded. My dear fellow, what good is caution? You can't learn every danger in advance. To be sure —" Now, you must know, I can get along with a man right up to his "to be sure"; for surely it goes without saying that every general rule has its exceptions. But the man is so terribly careful that the moment he thinks he's said something a bit too rash, too sweeping, only half true, he won't stop qualifying and trimming and whittling away until in the end there's nothing left of it at all. And on this occasion he got so deep into the text that I stopped listening to him altogether and fell to brooding, and with one sudden motion I pressed the muzzle of the pistol to my forehead, above the right eye. "Good God," cried Albert, pulling the pistol down, "what is this?" "It isn't loaded," I said. "Even so — what do you mean by it?" he snapped. "I can't imagine how a man could be foolish enough to shoot himself; the very thought disgusts me."

"But why is it," I said, "that whenever you people talk of some action, you have to come straight out with: this is foolish, that is clever, this is good, that is bad? And what does any of it mean? Have you really looked into the inner workings of an act? Can you account for the reasons, the necessity, that made it happen and had to make it happen? If you had, you wouldn't be so quick with your verdicts."
"But you'll grant me," said Albert, "that certain acts are wicked, whatever the motive behind them." I shrugged and let it pass.

"Still, my dear fellow," I went on, "even here there are exceptions. It's true that theft is a crime; but a man who steals to save himself and his family from starving — does he deserve pity or punishment? Who casts the first stone at the husband who in righteous fury kills his unfaithful wife and her worthless seducer? at the girl who, in one rapturous hour, loses herself in the irresistible joys of love? Even our laws, cold and pedantic as they are, let themselves be moved and hold back their punishment."
"That's a different matter entirely," said Albert, "because a man swept away by his passions loses all power of reflection and counts as a drunkard or a madman."

"Oh, you reasonable people!" I cried, smiling. "Passion! Drunkenness! Madness! There you stand, so cool, so unconcerned, you moral men — scolding the drunkard, loathing the madman, passing by on the other side like the priest, and thanking God like the Pharisee that he hasn't made you as one of them. I've been drunk more than once, my passions have never been far from madness, and I'm not ashamed of either; for I've learned, in my own way, that all extraordinary men who ever did something great, something that seemed impossible, have always been cried down as drunk or mad. And in ordinary life too it's unbearable to hear it said of nearly anyone who does a halfway free, noble, unexpected thing: the man is drunk, he's a fool! Shame on you sober ones, shame on you sages!"

"There you go again with your fancies," said Albert; "you overstrain everything, and here at least you're plainly wrong to set suicide, which is what we're talking about, beside great deeds — when it can't be seen as anything but a weakness. After all, it's easier to die than to bear a life of torment with backbone."

I was on the point of breaking it off, for nothing throws me off balance like having someone trot out an empty platitude while I'm speaking from the bottom of my heart. But I checked myself, since I'd heard it often enough and been vexed by it often enough, and answered him rather hotly: "You call it weakness? I beg you, don't be fooled by appearances. When a people groaning under a tyrant's unbearable yoke at last rises up and breaks its chains, will you call that weakness? And the man who, with his house in flames, feels his strength so doubled by terror that he easily carries off loads he could hardly stir when calm; the man who in the fury of an insult takes on six others and overpowers them — are these to be called weak? My good friend, if straining every nerve is strength, why should straining it to the utmost be the opposite?"

Albert looked hard at me and said, "Don't take it amiss, but the examples you bring up don't seem to fit the case at all." "That may be," I answered; "people have often told me my way of stringing things together verges on the muddled. So let's see if we can't picture another way how a man must feel who decides to throw off the otherwise pleasant burden of life. For only insofar as we can feel a thing with him do we have any right to speak of it.

"Human nature," I went on, "has its limits. It can bear joy, sorrow, pain up to a certain point, and is destroyed the moment that point is passed. So the question isn't whether a man is weak or strong, but whether he can endure the measure of his suffering — be it of the soul or the body. And I find it just as strange to call a man a coward for taking his own life as it would be to call a man a coward for dying of a deadly fever."

"Paradoxical! Quite paradoxical!" Albert exclaimed. "Not so much as you think," I replied. "You'll admit we call a sickness mortal when nature is so hard hit, her forces so far spent, that she can't pull herself together again, can't by any lucky turn set the ordinary course of life going once more."

"Now, my friend, carry that over to the mind. Look at a man in his narrow bounds: how impressions work on him, how fixed ideas take root, until at last a swelling passion robs him of all calm power of thought and destroys him."

"It's no use for a calm, reasonable man to take in the poor wretch's condition, no use for him to urge patience! Just as a healthy man standing at a sick man's bedside can't pour the least of his own strength into him."
To Albert this was all too general. I reminded him of a girl found drowned in the water not long before, and told him her story again:

"A good young creature, grown up inside the narrow round of household tasks and the week's set work, who knew no prospect of pleasure beyond strolling about town on a Sunday in the finery she'd slowly put together, with girls like herself, dancing perhaps at the great festivals, and otherwise gossiping for hours with a neighbor, all eagerness and warmth, over the cause of some quarrel or piece of slander. Then her fiery nature comes to feel deeper needs, fed by the flatteries of men; her old pleasures grow stale bit by bit, until at last she meets a man toward whom an unknown feeling draws her irresistibly, on whom she now pins all her hopes. She forgets the world around her, hears nothing, sees nothing, feels nothing but him, the one man, longs for nothing but him, the one man. Unspoiled by the empty pleasures of a fickle vanity, her longing drives straight at its goal: she means to be his, to find in an eternal bond all the happiness she lacks, to taste every joy she's pined for. Promises repeated again and again seal the certainty of all her hopes; bold caresses heighten her desires and hold her whole soul in thrall; she floats in a dull half-awareness, in a foretaste of every joy, strung to the highest pitch; she stretches out her arms at last to clasp all her wishes — and her lover leaves her. Numb, senseless, she stands at the edge of an abyss; everything is darkness around her, no prospect, no comfort, no inkling — for he has left her, the one in whom alone she felt her existence! She sees neither the wide world that lies before her, nor the many who might make good her loss; she feels herself alone, abandoned by all the world — and blind, hemmed in by the terrible need of her heart, she throws herself down to smother all her torments in death's encircling arms. There, Albert, is the story of many a one; and tell me, isn't this a case of sickness? Nature finds no way out of the maze of tangled, contradictory forces, and the human being must die."

"Woe to the man who can look on and say, 'The foolish girl!
